record_type_quote: This article reports a preregistered large-scale attempt to replicate four influential anticipatory-looking implicit theory-of-mind tasks using original stimuli and procedures.

targets.authors: Schneider, D., Bayliss, A. P., Becker, S. I., & Dux, P. E.
targets.title: Eye movements reveal sustained implicit processing of others’ mental states.
targets.evidence_quote: In the original studies, 14-month-old children (Surian & Geraci, 2012), adults (Schneider et al., 2012), or both children from the age of 2 years and adults (Low & Watts, 2013; Senju et al., 2009; Southgate et al., 2007) revealed anticipatory-looking patterns suggestive of belief-based anticipation in both their first looks and overall looking time. The current study exactly replicated the methods described in the original articles, using original stimuli and protocols, which were generously shared with us by the authors (for details, see Supplement A in the Supplemental Material available online).
targets.outcome_quote: The original results were thus only partially replicated: As in the original study, there was a significant Belief × Location interaction on looking times. But unlike in the original study, this was not due to the crucial difference in looking to the no-object location (participants looked longer to this location in the false-belief than in the truebelief condition).
targets.outcome_reasoning: Authors explicitly call these results partially replicated: the interaction agreed but the crucial no-object contrast did not; Study 2 produced the same pattern.

targets.title: Where will the triangle look for it? Attributing false beliefs to a geometric shape at 17 months.
targets.evidence_quote: In the original studies, 14-month-old children (Surian & Geraci, 2012), adults (Schneider et al., 2012), or both children from the age of 2 years and adults (Low & Watts, 2013; Senju et al., 2009; Southgate et al., 2007) revealed anticipatory-looking patterns suggestive of belief-based anticipation in both their first looks and overall looking time. The current study exactly replicated the methods described in the original articles, using original stimuli and protocols, which were generously shared with us by the authors (for details, see Supplement A in the Supplemental Material available online).
targets.outcome_quote: The Kulke et al. present study thus replicated only the original negative findings but not the positive ones.
targets.outcome_reasoning: Authors explicitly distinguish replicated null findings from positive findings that did not replicate.

targets.title: Attributing false beliefs about object identity reveals a signature blind spot in humans’ efficient mind-reading system.
targets.evidence_quote: In the original studies, 14-month-old children (Surian & Geraci, 2012), adults (Schneider et al., 2012), or both children from the age of 2 years and adults (Low & Watts, 2013; Senju et al., 2009; Southgate et al., 2007) revealed anticipatory-looking patterns suggestive of belief-based anticipation in both their first looks and overall looking time. The current study exactly replicated the methods described in the original articles, using original stimuli and protocols, which were generously shared with us by the authors (for details, see Supplement A in the Supplemental Material available online).
targets.outcome_quote: In sum, the original pattern of belief-congruent looking could be reproduced only under conditions in which the belief congruency of the locations is confounded with additional factors, and therefore, this pattern might not reflect belief-based anticipation.
targets.outcome_reasoning: The original materials yielded the effect, but the target-specific main message is that removing confounds eliminated belief-congruent anticipation and invalidated its interpretation as implicit theory of mind.

targets.authors: Southgate, V., Senju, A., & Csibra, G.
targets.title: Action anticipation through attribution of false belief by 2-year-olds.
targets.evidence_quote: In the original studies, 14-month-old children (Surian & Geraci, 2012), adults (Schneider et al., 2012), or both children from the age of 2 years and adults (Low & Watts, 2013; Senju et al., 2009; Southgate et al., 2007) revealed anticipatory-looking patterns suggestive of belief-based anticipation in both their first looks and overall looking time. The current study exactly replicated the methods described in the original articles, using original stimuli and protocols, which were generously shared with us by the authors (for details, see Supplement A in the Supplemental Material available online).
targets.outcome_quote: The overall original findings were not replicated, whereas a differential analysis of the False Belief 1 and False Belief 2 conditions suggests that only the False Belief 1 condition could be replicated.
targets.outcome_reasoning: An explicit overall verdict says the original findings were not replicated, despite success in False Belief 1.

reasoning: Four paradigms re-test five distinct published papers: the Southgate/Senju paradigm cites and tests findings from two papers. The adult sample re-tests age-general claims. Other cited replication papers are background, not targets. Outcomes use per-target explicit comparisons and aggregate the follow-up validity studies. DOI fields are empty because the reference entries print no DOIs. Study numbers in original papers are not specified; Low/Watts location condition is identified in a note.
